Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure.
  - 3 days of frequent loose, watery diarrhea with intermittent lower abdominal cramping.
  - Possible trigger: ate at a Chinese restaurant ~4 days ago; symptoms began ~1 day later.
  - Household: one child had vomiting (no diarrhea).
- Symptom timeline and progression.
  - Onset ~3 days ago; currently ~6–7 watery stools/day.
  - Initial vomiting at onset, now resolved.
  - Subjective fever/hot feeling at onset; no measured temperature; currently afebrile by report.
  - Feels weak/shaky; decreased appetite but tolerating fluids; eating soups/liquids.
- ENT symptoms (as applicable):
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: not discussed.
  - Voice change/hoarseness: not discussed.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia: not discussed.
  - Drooling: not discussed.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms: not discussed.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing: not discussed.
  - Dyspnea: not discussed.
  - Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling: not discussed.
  - Ear pain/hearing changes: not discussed.
  - Neck pain/swelling: not discussed.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments.
  - No prior similar episodes reported. No ED visits/hospitalizations reported.
- Allergies and current medications (mark missing dose/route/frequency as “not documented”).
  - Drug/food allergies: not documented.
  - Medications: asthma inhaler (type/dose/route/frequency not documented). No other medications.
- Any relevant social context.
  - Lives with wife and two children; works as an accountant; has continued working despite symptoms.
  - Nonsmoker; does not drink alcohol.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: not reported.
- Airway/breathing descriptors: no respiratory complaints reported; asthma stated as well-controlled.
- Mental status and associated features: reports weakness/shakiness; no dizziness/syncope reported.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient: not stated.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression: Acute gastroenteritis, likely infectious (viral > bacterial), after recent restaurant exposure; currently non-bloody diarrhea with improving vomiting and maintained oral intake.
- Evidence summary:
  - Watery, non-bloody diarrhea 6–7/day x 3 days, intermittent LLQ crampy pain.
  - Initial vomiting and subjective fever; vomiting resolved; tolerating fluids; decreased appetite.
  - Temporal association with restaurant meal (~24 hours later) and household contact with vomiting.
- DDx (aligned with transcript):
  1) Acute viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus) – Most likely: short course, vomiting at onset, sick contact with vomiting, non-bloody diarrhea, typically self-limited.
     - Opposing evidence: focal LLQ cramps; restaurant exposure could suggest bacterial etiology.
  2) Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/foodborne infection (e.g., Salmonella/ETEC/Campylobacter) – Possible: restaurant exposure with ~1-day incubation; fever and crampy pain compatible.
     - Opposing evidence: no blood/mucus; illness moderate and patient functional; household contact had only vomiting.
  3) Toxin-mediated food poisoning (Staph aureus/B. cereus) – Less likely: restaurant exposure and early vomiting fit, but typical incubation is hours and illness is usually brief; patient’s course is 3 days.
- No conflicts noted between transcript and DDx.

Plan:
- Immediate actions and advice:
  - Conservative management as discussed: maintain oral hydration; use oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) while diarrhea persists.
  - Analgesia/antipyretic: acetaminophen (paracetamol) as advised by clinician; “2 tablets up to four times daily” (tablet strength not documented).
  - Rest and time off work for 2–3 days to recover.
  - No antibiotics indicated at this time.
- Specific patient instructions:
  - Continue light foods as tolerated; prioritize fluids/electrolytes.
  - Practice hand hygiene to reduce household transmission.
- Escalation criteria/red flags:
  - Seek urgent care if any of the following develop: signs of dehydration (dizziness, confusion, minimal urine), persistent vomiting preventing fluid intake, high fever, blood or black stools, severe/worsening abdominal pain or localized peritoneal signs, or symptoms lasting >1 week.
- Follow-up:
  - Reassess in 3–4 days if not improving or sooner if worsening.
  - If ongoing, consider stool studies (pathogen PCR/culture) per clinician’s plan.

Quality checks:
● Missing but clinically expected elements for an acute ENT/allergy presentation: allergy list; detailed medication list with dose/route/frequency; review of ENT-specific symptoms (throat tightness, voice change, dysphagia, drooling, stridor/noisy breathing, facial/tongue/uvular swelling); documentation of dyspnea/wheezing; prior severe reactions or ED visits; availability of rescue devices (e.g., epinephrine auto-injector if relevant).  
● Additional clinical data not recorded but useful for this GI illness: vitals, physical exam (abdominal and hydration status), recent antibiotic use, recent travel, sick contacts beyond household, stool characteristics (mucus), and objective temperature.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none identified.  
● Transcript quality: generally clear; some filler words; no vitals or exam recorded.
